title: Seeing a threat — the heart-racing reflex
ask: Mia is walking home when a large dog runs at her, and her heart starts pounding. Explain the reflex arc behind this response: name each part (the eyes, the optic nerve, the parts of the brain, the cardiac nerves, the cardiac muscle) and say what each one does. (6 marks)
hook: EYE → NERVE II → BRAIN (see · fear · boss · heart centre) → SYMPATHETIC NERVE → HEART MUSCLE. The five parts in order: Real Sheep In My Engine (Receptor, Sensory, Integration, Motor, Effector).
steps: **Receptor = the EYES**: **photoreceptors** (rods and cones) in the **retina** detect the light from the threat and turn it into nerve impulses.
**Sensory (afferent) neuron = the OPTIC NERVE (cranial nerve II)**: carries the impulses from the eye into the brain.

**Integration centre = the BRAIN, part 1**: the **thalamus** relays the signal to the **visual cortex** in the **occipital lobe** (she sees it); the **limbic system (amygdala)** reads it as a threat, which is fear.
**Integration centre = the BRAIN, part 2**: the **hypothalamus** (the boss of the ANS) switches on the **sympathetic** division through the **cardioacceleratory centre** in the **medulla oblongata**.

**Motor (efferent) neuron = the SYMPATHETIC CARDIAC NERVES**: an autonomic **two-neuron pathway** (preganglionic → ganglion → postganglionic) from the thoracic spinal cord, releasing **norepinephrine** onto the heart.

**Effector = CARDIAC MUSCLE of the heart**: heart rate and force of contraction **increase**. It is an **autonomic (visceral) fight-or-flight reflex** because the effector is cardiac muscle, not skeletal muscle.

mcq.q: In the heart-racing reflex, which structure is the RECEPTOR?
d: The SA node of the heart
mcq.why: The receptor is where the stimulus is detected: the rods and cones of the retina pick up the light. The optic nerve only carries the signal afterwards.

mcq.q: Which TYPE of receptor starts this reflex?
mcq.why: The stimulus is light, i.e. seeing the dog, so photoreceptors. Nociceptors detect pain (the withdrawal reflex); proprioceptors detect stretch (the knee-jerk).

mcq.q: Which nerve is the SENSORY neuron in this arc?
mcq.why: Cranial nerve II, the optic nerve, is purely sensory (vision). The oculomotor nerve (III) MOVES the eye and is a common trap.

mcq.q: Which way does the optic nerve carry the impulse?
mcq.why: Sensory = afferent = towards the CNS. It brings the picture from the eye into the brain.

mcq.q: Which lobe holds the visual cortex that actually 'sees' the dog?
mcq.why: The visual cortex sits in the occipital lobe at the back of the brain. The temporal lobe does hearing; the frontal lobe does movement and reasoning.

mcq.q: Which part of the brain recognises the danger and produces fear?
mcq.why: The limbic system is the emotional brain, and its amygdala links to the hypothalamus for stress and fear. The cerebellum coordinates movement; the pineal gland makes melatonin.

mcq.q: Her slides call one structure the 'boss' of the autonomic nervous system. Which?
mcq.why: Her NS3 deck: the hypothalamus is the boss of the ANS and controls the medullary centres. The thalamus is only the sensory relay station.

mcq.q: Where is the cardioacceleratory centre that speeds up the heart?
mcq.why: Her NS3 deck lists the cardioacceleratory and cardioinhibitory centres (heart rate) in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem. The hypothalamus controls them from above.

mcq.q: Which division of the nervous system carries the 'speed up' signal to the heart?
mcq.why: Sympathetic = fight-or-flight: it raises heart rate. Parasympathetic fibres (vagus) SLOW the heart. Somatic motor neurons only supply skeletal muscle.

mcq.q: Which neurotransmitter do the sympathetic nerves release onto the heart?
mcq.why: Her NS3 slide 33: sympathetic fibres release norepinephrine (NE). Parasympathetic fibres release acetylcholine (ACh).

mcq.q: How many motor neurons link the spinal cord to the heart in this autonomic pathway?
mcq.why: The ANS is a two-neuron pathway: a preganglionic fibre to a ganglion, then a postganglionic fibre to the organ. A somatic motor pathway uses just one neuron.

mcq.q: Seeing the threat speeds up her pulse. What is the EFFECTOR?
mcq.why: The effector is whatever responds, and here the heart speeds up, so it is cardiac muscle. Running away would be a separate, voluntary action by skeletal muscle.

mcq.q: Why is this an AUTONOMIC reflex and not a somatic one?
mcq.a: The effector is cardiac muscle, not skeletal
d: The receptor is in the eye, not the skin
The brain is involved, not the spinal cord
The response is slow, not rapid
mcq.why: The effector decides the type. Somatic reflexes act on skeletal muscle; autonomic (visceral) reflexes act on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or glands. Plenty of somatic reflexes run through the brain, e.g. blinking.

mcq.q: Which other change belongs to this same sympathetic response?
mcq.why: Her NS3 slide 34, a person who is threatened: heart rate rises, breathing is rapid and deep, skin is cold and sweaty, pupils dilate. The other three are parasympathetic effects.

traps: Optic nerve (II) = SENSORY. Do not confuse it with the oculomotor nerve (III), which moves the eye.
SYMPATHETIC speeds the heart. The parasympathetic (vagus) SLOWS it; naming the vagus here loses the mark.
Say CARDIAC MUSCLE for the effector, and say why that makes it an AUTONOMIC reflex: the effector decides the type.
src: Her 2026 NS3 deck: slide 27 (the five components), slide 30 (visceral/autonomic reflexes regulate smooth and cardiac muscle), slides 32–34 (ANS two-neuron pathway, NE, 'a person who is threatened'), slide 38 (medulla cardioacceleratory centre; hypothalamus is the boss of the ANS); NS2 slide 23 notes (amygdala to hypothalamus: stress and fear).

title: Low blood calcium — homeostasis (PTH)
ask: Explain how the body restores homeostasis when the blood calcium level falls too low. Include the gland, the hormone and its target cells/organs, and how the response is switched off. (5 marks)
hook: PTH = Put The calcium Here (in the blood): Bone (osteoCLasts CLear bone), Kidneys (keep it), Gut (grab it). CalciTONin TONes it down: osteoBlasts Build it back into bone.
steps: **Stimulus**: blood **Ca²⁺ falls** below normal. This is a **humoral** stimulus (a chemical in the blood).
The **chief cells** of the **parathyroid glands** (4 tiny glands on the posterior thyroid) detect it and secrete **parathyroid hormone (PTH)** into the blood.
**Bone**: PTH stimulates **osteoclasts** to digest (resorb) bone matrix, releasing **Ca²⁺ into the blood**.
**Kidneys**: PTH makes the kidneys **reabsorb more Ca²⁺** (less is lost in urine) and activate vitamin D as **calcitriol**.
**Intestine**: more Ca²⁺ is **absorbed from food** by the intestinal mucosal cells.
**Negative feedback**: blood Ca²⁺ rises back to normal, and the rising Ca²⁺ **inhibits further PTH release**.

**The opposite arm**: HIGH blood Ca²⁺ makes the **parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid** release **calcitonin**, which inhibits osteoclasts so **osteoblasts** deposit Ca²⁺ in bone. Calcitonin is PTH's **antagonist**.

mcq.q: What kind of stimulus is a fall in blood calcium?
mcq.why: Humoral = a chemical level in the blood acts directly on the gland. 'Enzymatic' is her standing trap: there is no fourth type of stimulus.

mcq.q: Why does the body defend BLOOD calcium, even at the cost of bone?
mcq.a: Nerve conduction, muscle contraction and heart rhythm need it
d: It is the main buffer that keeps blood pH stable
It carries oxygen inside the red blood cells
It is the main fuel that cells turn into ATP
mcq.why: Her helpline: the body prioritises blood calcium because nervous conduction, muscle contraction and heart rhythm depend on it.

mcq.q: Which cells detect the low Ca²⁺ and release the calcium-raising hormone?
mcq.a: Chief cells of the parathyroid glands
d: Alpha cells of the pancreatic islets
mcq.why: Her Endocrine 2 slide 12: PTH is secreted by the chief cells. Parafollicular cells make calcitonin, the opposite hormone.

mcq.q: Where are the parathyroid glands?
mcq.why: Four tiny glands embedded in the back (posterior) of the thyroid. On top of the kidneys are the adrenals; below the hypothalamus is the pituitary.

mcq.q: Which bone cells does PTH stimulate to raise blood Ca²⁺?
mcq.why: OsteoCLasts CLear bone: they digest matrix and free its calcium. OsteoBlasts Build bone, which LOWERS blood calcium.

mcq.q: What do osteoclasts do when PTH stimulates them?
mcq.why: Resorption means breaking bone down so its stored Ca²⁺ goes into the blood. Depositing calcium and laying osteoid is osteoblast work.

mcq.q: What does PTH do at the kidneys?
mcq.why: PTH makes the kidneys keep calcium, so less leaves in the urine, and they activate vitamin D.

mcq.q: PTH makes the kidneys activate vitamin D. What is active vitamin D called?
mcq.why: Calcitriol (active vitamin D) helps RAISE blood calcium through the gut. Calcitonin sounds alike but LOWERS it.

mcq.q: Which THREE targets does PTH act on, directly or through calcitriol?
mcq.why: Her slide 13 lists the three: osteoclasts in bone, reabsorption in the kidneys, absorption by the intestinal mucosa.

mcq.q: What switches PTH secretion off again?
mcq.why: Her slide 12: rising blood Ca²⁺ inhibits PTH release and low Ca²⁺ stimulates it. The response removes its own stimulus, which is negative feedback.

mcq.q: Which hormone LOWERS blood calcium?
mcq.why: Calcitonin is the antagonist of PTH: it moves calcium from the blood into bone. PTH and calcitriol both raise blood calcium.

mcq.q: Calcitonin is released by which cells?
d: Chief cells of the parathyroid glands
Beta cells of the pancreatic islets
mcq.why: Her deck: parafollicular cells produce calcitonin, while the thyroid follicles make T3/T4. Chief cells make PTH.

mcq.q: Calcitonin lowers blood Ca²⁺ mainly by…
mcq.a: Inhibiting osteoclasts so Ca²⁺ stays in bone
d: Raising Ca²⁺ absorption from the gut
mcq.why: Her deck: calcitonin targets the skeleton, inhibits osteoclast activity and stimulates calcium deposition into bone matrix.

mcq.q: A 65-year-old has had low blood calcium for years. What is happening to her bones?
mcq.a: Resorbed to keep blood Ca²⁺ up: osteoporosis
d: Built up by osteoblasts: denser bone
mcq.why: Her car-accident case: PTH keeps pulling calcium out of bone, so density falls (osteopenia, then osteoporosis) and bones break easily and heal slowly.

traps: Name the CELLS: chief cells of the parathyroid (PTH) and parafollicular cells of the thyroid (calcitonin). 'The thyroid makes PTH' is wrong.
OsteoCLasts CLear bone (blood Ca²⁺ goes UP); osteoBlasts Build bone (blood Ca²⁺ goes DOWN). Swapping them loses the mark.
Calcitriol (active vitamin D, raises Ca²⁺) is not calcitonin (lowers Ca²⁺).
src: Her 2026 Endocrine 2 deck: slide 12 (PTH, chief cells, 4 glands on the posterior thyroid, negative feedback, humoral stimulus), slide 13 (the three PTH functions), the calcitonin slides (parafollicular cells, antagonist to PTH, inhibits osteoclasts); her helpline BLOOD CALCIUM and calcium-table answers; her Practice SAQ page.

title: Neuroglia — name 2 and how they protect the CNS
ask: Name TWO neuroglial cells of the central nervous system and explain how each one protects the CNS. (4 marks)
hook: CNS glia = A MOE: Astrocytes (BBB), Microglia (eat germs), Oligodendrocytes (myelin), Ependymal (CSF). PNS glia both start with S (Schwann, Satellite), and S stays Outside.
steps: **Astrocytes** (star-shaped): wrap the brain's capillaries to maintain the **blood-brain barrier (BBB)**, blocking **toxins, pathogens and large molecules** in the blood from reaching the neurons (chemical protection).
**Microglia**: the CNS's **immune defence cells**. They **phagocytose** (engulf and digest) bacteria, viruses, dead cells and foreign material.
**Ependymal cells**: ciliated cells **lining the ventricles**. In the **choroid plexuses** they **produce CSF**, and their cilia keep it moving. CSF cushions the brain against physical shock.
**Oligodendrocytes**: wrap CNS axons in **myelin**, an insulating layer that **protects the axons** and allows fast **saltatory conduction** (node of Ranvier to node) without short-circuiting.

**Not CNS**: **Schwann cells** (myelin in the PNS) and **satellite cells** (around neuron cell bodies in PNS ganglia) earn nothing in a CNS question. The safest pair to write is **astrocytes + microglia**.

mcq.q: Which glial cell maintains the blood-brain barrier?
mcq.why: Her helpline: star-shaped astrocytes maintain the BBB, wrapped around the capillaries to keep the seal tight.

mcq.q: How do astrocytes protect the neurons?
mcq.a: They seal capillaries against toxins and pathogens
d: They engulf bacteria and dead cell debris
They wrap axons in an insulating myelin layer
They line the ventricles and move the CSF
mcq.why: Astrocytes give chemical protection by keeping the BBB tight. Each wrong option is another glial cell's job: microglia, oligodendrocytes, ependymal cells.

mcq.q: Which CNS glial cell is the brain's immune defence?
mcq.why: Microglia are the CNS's own phagocytes. The brain sits behind the BBB, so it needs its own immune cells.

mcq.q: What do microglia do to protect the CNS?
d: Produce CSF in the choroid plexus
mcq.why: Microglia engulf (phagocytose) invaders and dead cells. Sealing the BBB is astrocyte work; myelin is oligodendrocyte work.

mcq.q: Which glial cells line the ventricles and make CSF?
mcq.why: Ependymal cells are ciliated and line the ventricles; specialised ones in the choroid plexuses produce CSF.

mcq.q: How does the CSF made by ependymal cells protect the brain?
mcq.a: Cushions it and flushes away waste
d: Kills bacteria that cross the BBB
mcq.why: CSF is a shock absorber (the brain floats in it) and it rinses waste away. Killing bacteria is microglia; insulation is myelin; sealing is astrocytes.

mcq.q: Which cell forms myelin in the CNS?
mcq.why: CNS myelin comes from oligodendrocytes and PNS myelin from Schwann cells. Her Practice SAQ asks exactly this contrast.

mcq.q: Myelin speeds conduction because the impulse jumps between the…
mcq.why: Saltatory conduction: the impulse leaps from one node of Ranvier (a gap in the myelin) to the next.

mcq.q: A question asks you to name CNS neuroglia. Which answer earns NO mark?
mcq.why: Schwann cells are PNS glia. The CNS four are astrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells and oligodendrocytes.

mcq.q: Where are satellite cells found?
mcq.a: Around cell bodies in PNS ganglia
d: Lining the ventricles of the brain
Around axons in the spinal cord
mcq.why: Satellite cells surround neuron cell bodies in the PNS ganglia. They are PNS glia, so they are not an answer for the CNS.

traps: Schwann cells and satellite cells are PNS glia, so they earn no marks in a CNS question.
Microglia are ONE type of neuroglia; 'glia' covers all the support cells. Write two DIFFERENT cells.
A name alone is half the marks. Give each cell AND its protective job (e.g. astrocytes: keep the BBB tight).
src: Her helpline BRAIN & SPINAL CORD PROTECTION answers (astrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells, oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, satellite cells, in her wording); her Practice SAQ page ('What cells form myelin in the CNS and what cells form myelin in the PNS?').

title: The reflex arc — 5 parts, somatic vs autonomic
ask: Describe the five components of a reflex arc. Then explain the difference between a somatic and an autonomic reflex, giving an example of each with its receptor and effector. (5 marks)
hook: Real Sheep In My Engine: Receptor, Sensory, Integration, Motor, Effector. Skeletal muscle = somatic; smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or gland = autonomic.
steps: **Receptor**: the site of the stimulus, which detects the change (e.g. **nociceptors** for pain, **proprioceptors** for stretch).
**Sensory (afferent) neuron**: carries the impulse **to the CNS**.
**Integration centre**: inside the **CNS** (spinal cord or brainstem), monosynaptic or polysynaptic through an **interneuron**. It is hard-wired, so no conscious thought is needed.
**Motor (efferent) neuron**: carries the impulse **away from the CNS** to the effector.
**Effector**: the **muscle or gland** that responds with a rapid, predictable, **involuntary** response.
**Somatic reflex**: the effector is **skeletal muscle**, e.g. the **withdrawal reflex** (nociceptors) or the **stretch / knee-jerk reflex** (proprioceptors).
**Autonomic (visceral) reflex**: the effector is **smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or a gland**, e.g. the **pupillary light reflex** (smooth muscle of the iris) or the heart speeding up.

mcq.q: What is the FIRST component of every reflex arc?
mcq.why: The order is receptor, sensory neuron, integration centre, motor neuron, effector. Nothing happens until a receptor detects the stimulus.

mcq.q: Which receptors start the withdrawal reflex?
mcq.why: Her NS3 slide 28: withdrawal reflex, RECEPTORS = NOCICEPTORS (pain). Proprioceptors belong to the stretch reflex.

mcq.q: Which receptors start the stretch (knee-jerk) reflex?
mcq.why: Her NS3 slide 29: stretch reflex, RECEPTORS = PROPRIOCEPTORS, which sense the muscle being stretched.

mcq.q: Which neuron carries the impulse TOWARDS the CNS?
mcq.why: Afferent = arrives at the CNS. Efferent = exits the CNS towards the effector.

mcq.q: In a spinal reflex, where does integration happen?
mcq.a: Grey matter of the spinal cord
d: White matter of the spinal cord
mcq.why: The interneurons and cell bodies are in the grey matter (the butterfly). White matter is the axon tracts carrying signals up and down.

mcq.q: Why does a reflex not need conscious thought?
mcq.a: It is hard-wired in the spinal cord by interneurons
d: The cortex makes the decision very quickly
The effector reacts without any neurons
Hormones carry the message to the muscle
mcq.why: Her learning page: the response is the same every time, so it is hard-wired into the spinal cord with interneurons and the brain is not needed to decide.

mcq.q: Which component carries efferent impulses to the effector organ?
mcq.why: Her slide 27: the motor neuron conducts efferent impulses from the integration centre to the effector organ.

mcq.q: In the knee-jerk reflex, what is the effector?
mcq.why: Tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps, which contracts and kicks the leg out. The effector is the muscle that responds.

mcq.q: Which reflex is SOMATIC?
mcq.why: Somatic = skeletal muscle: pulling your hand off a hot pan. The other three act on smooth or cardiac muscle, so they are autonomic (her slide 30).

mcq.q: Which reflex is AUTONOMIC (visceral)?
mcq.why: Her slide 30: visceral reflexes regulate smooth and cardiac muscle and glands, e.g. micturition, defaecation, pupillary light and baroreceptor reflexes.

mcq.q: The pupillary light reflex is autonomic because its effector is the…
mcq.why: The iris muscles are smooth muscle, and smooth muscle means an autonomic reflex. Photoreceptors are the receptor, not the effector.

traps: The interneuron IS the integration centre in a spinal reflex. Write both: 'integration centre (interneuron) in the spinal cord'.
Receptor detects; effector responds. Keep them apart.
The EFFECTOR decides the type: skeletal muscle = somatic; smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or gland = autonomic.
src: Her 2026 NS3 deck slides 26–30 (definition, five components, somatic withdrawal/stretch reflexes with their receptors, visceral reflexes); her 'Spinal Nerves and the Reflex Arc' learning page; her Practice SAQ page ('Describe the 5 steps of a reflex arc (2.5 marks)'; the receptors of the withdrawal and stretch reflexes).
